title: Surprising increase in yield stress of Mg single crystal using long-period stacking ordered nanoplates

With twinning suppressed and basal slip geometrically unable to accommodate the load, plasticity is taken up by kink banding: basal dislocations aligned into band boundaries

requires_unseen: kink boundary described as an alignment of basal dislocations (Fig. 5 linked text, refs 21,42-46)

nodes.label: The crystal keeps a yield stress above 100 MPa with more than 5% compressive plastic strain in [11-20] and [01-10] from RT to 400 C

source_checked.why: the line I applied: caption facts that identify the panel - technique, specimen, condition, viewing direction, which panel is which - are how every packet works and are recorded in image_note; they do not by themselves force source != figure. A fact forces it when the label carries a value no panel yields, an identification made by an analysis absent from the packet, or a statement about material the packet never shows. So n20 keeps figure although '(0001)' follows from the caption's [11-20] viewing direction, and n14/o18/o19 keep figure although 'pure Mg' for #F7b is a caption fact: the 5-10x ratio is computable from the two panels, which share identical axes.

pairs.effect: Formation of thin stacking-fault-like defects named LPSO nanoplates parallel to the basal plane
pairs.note: n6 (PRC/forming, DS growth) -produces-> n8 (the planar defects are LPSO nanoplates: aggregated four-layer Zn/Y-segregated fcc-type faults) and -produces-> n20 (plates parallel to (0001), heterogeneously dispersed). Evidence o1 (SEM traces on one alignment), o2 (g=0002 contrast that a conventional R=1/3<10-10> fault could not give, with n25 as the invisibility premise) and o3 (HAADF bright heavy-atom bands). MatMech's Bridgman technique and 5.0 mm/h growth rate appear nowhere in the packet and are correctly absent from the graph; the ~28 nm thickness and ~9.8 per um density it quotes are n9 and o5.

pairs.cause: Presence of LPSO nanoplates parallel to the basal plane
pairs.effect: Drastic increase in yield stress compared to pure Mg
pairs.note: n9 (nanoplate density and thickness set by heat treatment) -causes-> n12, explained by n15 (twinning and non-basal slip must cut the (0001) plates while basal slip glides parallel), whose geometric premise is n20. The decisive readout is o20, the 167 -> 113 -> 160 MPa swing that follows the density, and n14/o18 give the selective CRSS rise MatMech's 'barriers to common deformation modes' asserts. Two record notes: MatMech calls the [0001] number a yield stress of >350 MPa, while the graph (o6, n21) records ~355 MPa as a fracture stress reached without yielding; and MatMech's 'compared to pure Mg' uses the text's ~11x, which n12 now carries as a requires_unseen fact because the panel reads ~148-165 MPa.

pairs.cause: High yield stress due to LPSO nanoplates
pairs.effect: Enhanced ductility and strength during plastic deformation due to kink-band formation
pairs.note: Both ends are in the graph and connected: n12 -supports-> n17 (above 100 MPa with more than 5% compressive plastic strain, RT to 400 C, evidence o8 and now o7) and n16 (kink banding takes up plasticity once twinning is suppressed and basal slip cannot accommodate the load, evidence o21) -supports-> n18 (~45% tensile elongation by kinking, o23, o24), with n11 the kink-band identification. MatMech's own deductive line - 'LPSO nanoplates induce kink-band formation, enabling both high strength and ductility' - is n15 -> n16 exactly. The one direction nuance: the graph does not make the high yield stress the cause of the ductility; it makes the nanoplates, through n15, the common cause of both, which is the stronger reading of the same pair. n23 records that the tensile number understates the kink-band stress.
